$comment: Shared authorization conformance cases. THE contract for the two-tier model.
The policy is implemented twice — boards/authz.mjs (Node: CLI + UI server) and
of a permission check is how surfaces come to disagree, and a disagreement here is
a security bug rather than a routing quirk. So neither implementation owns the
behaviour: this file does, and both test suites assert against it.
Adding a case is how you change the policy. Change an implementation without
changing this file and the other implementation's suite still passes, which is
exactly the drift this exists to prevent.
`agent: null` means an unidentified caller. Absent `resource` means none applies.

cases.name: user reads any board
admin reads any board
user may create and update items
admin may create and update items
user deletes an item it created
user cannot delete another agent's item
user cannot delete an item with no recorded creator
cases.$why: Treating unattributed as owned would expose every item predating creator attribution.

cases.name: admin deletes another agent's item
admin deletes an unattributed item
a user may mint a user invite — sign-up is open
cases.$why: Not a secret system. Gating sign-up would only mean a human must find someone with a CLI before their agent can be honest about its own name.

cases.name: mint_invite with no role named is a user invite
a user may NOT mint an admin invite
cases.$why: The one exception to open sign-up. Otherwise anyone self-promotes past the delete rules in one step and the tier is decorative.

cases.name: escalation attempt is caught regardless of casing or padding
cases.$why: normalizeRole maps anything unrecognized to `user`, which is right for reading a stored row and wrong here — ' ADMIN ' must be checked, not quietly downgraded to an open sign-up.

cases.name: an admin may mint an admin invite
an admin may also mint a user invite
a revoked user may not mint even a user invite
cases.$why: Revocation outranks the openness of sign-up, or revoking would not stop anything.

cases.name: user may delegate a user child
anonymous may not delegate
user delegation caps requested admin child to user
user cannot manage agents
admin manages agents
user cannot manage silos
admin manages silos
revoked admin cannot manage silos
cases.$why: Revocation must outrank tier, or revoking an admin would be cosmetic.

cases.name: user may call the roster (scoped to itself)
admin may call the roster
unidentified caller cannot read
unidentified caller cannot write
unidentified caller cannot delete even an unowned item
revoked admin loses every privilege
cases.$why: Revocation must outrank tier, or revoking an admin would be cosmetic.

cases.name: revoked user cannot even read
unknown role falls back to user, not admin
cases.$why: A row written by a newer build with a role this one does not know must fail closed.

cases.name: empty role falls back to user
role match is case-insensitive
unknown action is refused for an admin
cases.$why: Fail closed on actions an older build has no policy for.

$comment_decide: `decide` cases cover the unidentified-caller policy. A surface declares a stance:
operator  — unrestricted (the CLI: local trust root, and the only path that can
mint the first invite, so it cannot be read-only without making the
read_only — may read every board, may change nothing (the browser, where a login
box makes presenting a credential a real affordance)
deny      — refuse outright (a hosted deployment; FEADS_REQUIRE_AGENT=1)
`require_identity: true` is an alias for stance `deny`. Absent stance = operator,
which is the pre-existing behaviour of every surface that passes nothing.
An identified caller ignores the stance entirely — its tier decides.

decide_cases.name: unidentified caller is the operator by default
unidentified caller is refused when identity is required
decide_cases.$why: Mode is `anonymous`, not `operator`: a refused caller was never granted operator standing, and reporting one would misdescribe why it was denied.

decide_cases.name: identified user still cannot delete another's item in operator-permissive mode
decide_cases.$why: The flag governs unidentified callers only; presenting an identity opts you into your tier.

decide_cases.name: identified admin deletes another's item
revoked agent is denied even with the flag off
a rejected credential is denied, not treated as the operator
decide_cases.$why: The permissive fallback would invert revocation: a revoked user would become the operator and gain the ability to delete anything. Revoking would promote.

decide_cases.name: a rejected credential cannot even read
rejection outranks the require_identity flag being off or on
a resolved agent ignores the rejected flag entirely
decide_cases.$why: If an agent resolved, its credential verified; the flag can only describe a failed resolution.

decide_cases.name: read_only: an anonymous caller may read every board
decide_cases.$why: The browser stance. Gating a look would be a ceremony that changes nothing about what a local shell can do.

decide_cases.name: read_only: an anonymous caller may not write
read_only: an anonymous caller may not delete, even an unowned item
read_only: an anonymous caller may not manage agents
read_only: an anonymous caller may not manage silos
read_only: an anonymous visitor MAY sign up
decide_cases.$why: The one write an anonymous visitor may cause. Requiring an identity to get an identity is a closed loop.

decide_cases.name: read_only: an anonymous visitor signing up cannot ask for admin
decide_cases.$why: Otherwise sign-up is a self-promotion button and the tier means nothing.

decide_cases.name: deny stance keeps sign-up open — enrollment is how a caller satisfies the requirement
decide_cases.$why: Closing sign-up under deny made the stance unescapable from the dashboard (an identity is needed to get an identity). The hosted deployment sits behind platform SSO, so the door itself is already gated; the login route is ungated for the same reason.

decide_cases.name: deny stance still refuses an admin invite
decide_cases.$why: Open sign-up must never be a self-promotion button — same rule as read_only.

decide_cases.name: operator may mint an admin invite — this is the bootstrap path
decide_cases.$why: The first admin can only come from here. If this ever fails, no board can get its first admin.

decide_cases.name: read_only: an identified user is unaffected by the stance
decide_cases.$why: The stance describes unidentified callers only; a token opts you into your tier.

decide_cases.name: read_only: a rejected credential is still rejected, not read-only
decide_cases.$why: Rejection outranks every stance — otherwise a revoked agent would quietly land in the anonymous bucket.

decide_cases.name: deny stance refuses even a read
require_identity is an alias for the deny stance
an unknown stance falls back to operator, not to deny
decide_cases.$why: Failing closed here would break the CLI on a typo, which is worse than the typo. Unknown input must not silently change a working surface.

decide_cases.name: an absent stance is operator, preserving pre-existing behaviour

$comment_resolution: How a surface works out WHO is calling, before any policy question is asked.
Resolution is as security-sensitive as the policy and was drifting between surfaces:
the CLI refused a token that would not verify while the UI treated it as merely
unidentified — which locally means operator, so revoking an agent PROMOTED it.
`token`: absent | invalid | valid. `session`: absent | no_match | live | revoked.
Expected: which credential won (`via`), whether an agent resolved, and whether a
credential was presented and refused (`credential_rejected`, which then feeds
`decide`). Node: resolveAgentIdentity in boards/agents.mjs. Python: the MCP's
equivalent. Both must satisfy every row.

resolution_cases.name: a valid token wins even when a session would also match
an invalid token is a rejection
an invalid token is NOT rescued by a session that would have matched
resolution_cases.$why: An explicitly presented credential that fails must not fall back to a weaker one that succeeds, or revoking a token would be defeated by the session id sitting next to it.

resolution_cases.name: a session matching a live agent resolves it
a session matching a REVOKED agent is a rejection
resolution_cases.$why: The common door for a long-lived daemon: no token, but always a session id. Treating this as 'never registered' is what makes revocation promote an agent to operator.

resolution_cases.name: a session matching nothing is not a rejection
resolution_cases.$why: Claude Code exports CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID into every session whether or not anyone registered, so this must stay merely unidentified or nearly every caller is denied.

resolution_cases.name: nothing presented at all is merely unidentified

$comment_roster_scope_for: `rosterScopeFor` is what surfaces call: the tier lookup plus the operator rule.
An operator run through the plain tier lookup resolves to `none` and shows an EMPTY
roster, which reads as 'no agents registered' rather than 'you were not recognized'.

roster_scope_for_cases.name: unidentified caller sees nothing when identity is required
an identified user still sees only itself
a revoked agent sees nothing even in permissive mode
roster_scope_for_cases.$why: Presenting a revoked identity must not fall through to operator.

roster_scope_for_cases.name: a rejected credential sees nothing, not the whole roster
a read-only anonymous caller sees no roster at all
roster_scope_for_cases.$why: Who else is registered is administrative data; it does not ride along with read-only board access.

roster_scope_for_cases.name: an operator still sees the whole roster

roster_scope_cases.name: revoked admin sees nothing, not everything
roster_scope_cases.$why: Revocation outranks tier here too, so a stale credential cannot read the roster.
